w: Built in 1836 on the site of a 7th-century predecessor, this Neoclassical church is San Marino's main church, its porch ringed by eight Corinthian columns. Dedicated to founder Saint Marinus, it holds his relics and serves as co-cathedral of the Diocese of San Marino-Montefeltro.
s: Neoclassical co-cathedral holding the founder's relics
_facts: Built 1836 on a 7th-century church site
Neoclassical style, porch of eight Corinthian columns
Holds relics of Saint Marinus, the republic's founder
Co-cathedral of the Diocese of San Marino-Montefeltro

w: Opera house designed by Luigi Poletti, opened in 1857 with the world premiere of Verdi's Aroldo. Rebuilt after the 1916 earthquake and again after WWII bombing left it half-destroyed, it was renamed in 1947 and fully restored by 2018 -- 800 seats across three tiers of boxes and a gallery.
s: Rimini's opera house, rebuilt twice, still hosting Verdi
_facts: Opened 1857 with world premiere of Verdi's Aroldo
Damaged in 1916 earthquake and WWII bombing
Renamed for composer Amintore Galli in 1947
Fully restored, reopened 2018; seats 800

w: Rimini's civic museum occupies a former Jesuit convent on Via Luigi Tonini, next to the Chiesa del Suffragio. Its modern annexe in Piazza Ferrari, the Domus del Chirurgo archaeological complex, encloses the excavated ruins of an ancient Roman house.
s: Civic museum built around a Roman surgeon's house
_facts: Housed in a former Jesuit convent, Via Luigi Tonini
Adjoins the Chiesa del Suffragio
Annexe encloses ruins of a Roman domus (Domus del Chirurgo)

w: Commonwealth war cemetery in Coriano holding 1,939 burials, about 50 unidentified, from the Allied advance through the Valconca and the battles of Coriano and Rimini in 1944. Managed by the CWGC's Rome office, it ranks among Coriano's most-visited sites -- headstones on the ridge the Allies fought to take.
s: 1,939 Commonwealth graves from the battle for Rimini
_facts: 1,939 burials, ~50 unidentified
For Allied dead in the Coriano and Rimini battles, 1944
Managed by the CWGC's Rome office
One of Coriano's most-visited sites

w: Renaissance church built 1553-1575 beside a Benedictine abbey, replacing a 9th-century predecessor. Napoleon suppressed the Benedictines in 1797, but the art stayed: Paolo Veronese's Martyrdom of San Giuliano (1588) hangs as the main altarpiece, alongside a 1409 polyptych by Bittino da Faenza.
s: A Veronese altarpiece survives Napoleon's Benedictines
_facts: Built 1553-1575 on a 9th-century church site
Benedictine order suppressed here in 1797
Main altarpiece: Veronese's Martyrdom of San Giuliano, 1588
Also holds a 1409 polyptych by Bittino da Faenza

w: Tucked inside the Cesta, the second of San Marino's towers, this arms museum opened in 1956 after a deal with local collector Giovanni Carlo Giorgetti. About 2,000 historic arms and suits of armour fill four rooms, part of the state museum network -- a private hoard turned public inside a medieval tower.
s: 2,000 antique weapons inside a medieval watchtower
_facts: Opened 1956 via deal with collector Giovanni Carlo Giorgetti
Housed inside the Cesta tower
~2,000 arms and armour across four rooms
Part of San Marino's Musei di Stato

w: Founded in 1689 with a marble altar donated by musician Antonio Tedeschi and a statue of St Peter by Enrico Saroldi. Its crypt holds two niches tradition calls the beds of Saints Marino and Leo. In 1849 Garibaldi and Anita hid here fleeing the fallen Roman Republic; a state monument to Pope John XXIII stands inside.
s: Where Garibaldi hid, and two saints once slept
_facts: Founded 1689; altar donated by Antonio Tedeschi
Crypt niches traditionally called the beds of Saints Marino and Leo
Garibaldi and Anita sheltered here in 1849
Contains a state-erected monument to Pope John XXIII

w: Built from 1969 and opened to worshippers in 1971, this Poor Clares monastery in the Valdragone curazia replaced an older convent from 1565. Its 17 nuns relocated from the City of San Marino; the rebuilding was pushed through by Bishop Costantino Bonelli.
s: Clarisse nuns' convent, rebuilt on 400-year-old ground
_facts: Current building 1969-1971, replacing an older 1565 convent
Home to 17 nuns of the Poor Clares (Clarisses)
Located in the Valdragone curazia of Borgo Maggiore
Rebuilding promoted by Bishop Costantino Bonelli

w: Public library founded in 1619 on a bequest from Riminese lawyer Alessandro Gambalunga. Known locally as the Gambalunghiana, it now holds over 300,000 items, including nearly 294,000 books -- and a reader list that runs from Ezra Pound to art historian Aby Warburg.
s: A 1619 library once read by Ezra Pound
_facts: Founded 1619 on a bequest from Alessandro Gambalunga
Over 300,000 items, including ~293,879 books (Dec 2023)
Documented readers include Ezra Pound and Aby Warburg

w: Baroque church of the Theatine order, flattened in the bombardments before the 1944 Battle of Rimini. Only the ruined apse interior survives, standing in the park that took the church's place -- a plaque is all that names what used to stand here.
s: A plaque marks a Baroque church bombed to ruins
_facts: Baroque-style Theatine church
Destroyed by bombing before the 1944 Battle of Rimini
Only apse ruins remain, in a park on the site
Marked today by a plaque
